I just finished reading Atlas Shrugged by Ayn Rand. I’d been putting it off because any time it comes up in conversation it gets dismissed as "that crazy Libertarian book." I assumed it would be a political manifesto. While it definitely makes a strong political statement, it also deals with much more. It celebrates reason and self-actualization over entitlement and feelings-based-politics. The entire book is excellent, but a couple quotes in particular stood out to me.

He had never spared himself in any issue. When a problem came up... his first concern was to discover what error he had made; he did not search for anyone’s fault but his own; it was of himself that he demanded perfection.

This is one of the core principles that distinguishes the red pill community from any other discussion of gender dynamics: personal responsibility. Nobody owes you success, or sex, or happiness; you have to make those things for yourself. On the flip side, if you’re not having success with women, that’s your fault. Women aren’t evil bitches out to get you, they’re following their natures. The only thing you can change is your own behavior. The only place you can effectively lay blame is on yourself.

"If you can refute a single sentence I uttered, madame, I shall hear it gratefully."
"Oh, I can’t answer you. I don’t have any answers, my mind doesn’t work that way, but I don’t feel that you’re right, so I know that you’re wrong."

There are some passages where Rand is subtle with her message. This is not one of them. Such a flippant response to a logical argument is ridiculous almost the point of caricature. What makes it stand out, though, is that it’s not caricature. The cultural acceptance of feelings over reasoned argument is quite frankly terrifying. (I saw an article just the other day about the the dehumanizing effects of meritocracy. You know who gets upset by meritocracy? People with no merit.)

Well, the man who despises himself tries to gain self-esteem from from sexual adventures - which can’t be done, because sex is not the cause, but an effect and an expression of a man’s sense of his own value.

Another idea TRP helped hammer home for me. If you don’t have a strong sense of your own self-worth, sex won’t give it to you. Sure it may give you a brief bump, but in the long run it still feels hollow. Value has to come from you and the sense of achievement you feel when working toward your goals. Once you have that innate sense of value, holding frame and staying on mission around women becomes easy. Cultivating personal value is the key to the kingdom. If you build it, they will come (so to speak).

Overall, it’s a compelling story and covers a lot of red pill ideas. Not to mention in virtually every sex scene, Rand describes the heroine’s thrill when a high value man takes over "without requiring her consent." Written by a woman. In 1957. If you haven’t read it, or haven’t read it since discovering the red pill, I cannot recommend it highly enough.

Well, there's a reason college guys go through their "Rand Phase"...Fountainhead is a better novel, whereas Shrugged becomes didactic to the point of bogging down as this 1,000+ page book plows on. Rands ideas are very cogent all by themselves, but the real world around us is too complex for Objectivism to work well as a creed for living. Americans live in a nation with 321,034,355 people in it, give or take, and we will never have a laissez-faire capitalist system in place. We will always have some sort of mixed economy. Moral compromises and pragmatic choices will always need to be made as things change. At this point, Rand should be read because her ideas are part of the culture, but having a critical eye is key. Even her former protege Nathaniel Branden pointed out that "she really had the right to be wrong sometimes."

I've heard a lot of conflicting thoughts as to why or why not Brady will succeed in Federal court. The two major opponent lines of reasoning go 1) He can't take it to court because he's guilty and he can't disclose his phone and 2) Even if he takes it to court Goodell followed the rules set forth by the CBA, nothing the NFL did is illegal.

For the first one, it's pretty obvious that this is a binary "either Brady is comfortable with disclosing his phone or not" and not really worth discussing, it just depends on whether or not you think he did it.

I think the second one is more interesting. In Brady's appeal letter, the NFLPA states that Troy Vincent wasn't even authorized to hand down a condruct detrimental discipline, and therefore it should have been directly from the commissioner, who then could not sit as the arbitrator, as seen here: "The CBA grants the Commissioner—and only the Commissioner—the authority to impose conduct detrimental discipline on players. CBA, Art. 46, § 1(a); id., App. A, ¶ 15. This express CBA mandate is further confirmed by the “law of the shop.” See Rice Art. 46 Appeal Decision (“Rice”) at 15; Bounty Art. 46 Appeal Decision (“Bounty”) at 4. Indeed, whereas the CBA expressly authorizes the Commissioner to delegate his authority to serve as Hearing Officer over Article 46 appeals, after consultation with the NFLPA, it contains no corresponding provision authorizing the Commissioner to delegate his exclusive role to impose conduct detrimental discipline to you or anyone else. You have no authority to impose discipline on Mr. Brady under the CBA, and such discipline must therefore be set aside."

In Goodell's response letter, he writes that 1, the discipline IS IN FACT commissioner discipline as stated here:

"First, the NFLPA argues that I may not serve as hearing officer because Mr. Brady's discipline letter was signed by NFL executive vice president Troy Vincent rather than by me. I disagree. The identity of the person who signed the disciplinary letter is irrelevant. The signatory's identity does not influence in any way my evaluation of the issues; any suggestion to the contrary defies common sense. (I note that NFL executives other than the Commissioner have signed disciplinary letters in numerous proceedings in which the Commissioner or his designee later served as hearing officer. I am not aware of any objections by the Union to that practice. To the contrary, as Mr. Nash's letter points out, the Union has confirmed its acceptance of this procedure.)

There can be no dispute that this is an appeal of Commissioner discipline: As the letter signed by Mr. Vincent explains in its first sentence, "The Commissioner has authorized me to inform you of the discipline that, pursuant to his authority under Article 46 of the CBA, has been imposed upon you ... ." I did not delegate my disciplinary authority to Mr. Vincent; I concurred in his recommendation and authorized him to communicate to Mr. Brady the discipline imposed under my authority as Commissioner."

and secondly that he can sit as arbitrator because: "the CBA provides that "the Commissioner may serve as hearing officer in "any appeal" involving conduct detrimental to the integrity of the game."

So my question is, is this a total loophole he only pulled out for Brady, or is this bullshit? Where is it written that the issuer of the punishment can't be the arbiter in the CBA? Can Brady win in court simply on this? Or would he stick with attacking the science? OR would he have to prove the NFL is out to defame him, which would be the hardest and worst case scenarios? I feel like I've heard legal analysts saying all three...
Thoughts on Brady's chances in court?

Well I wouldn't have a very informed opinion on this myself but I'm willing to bet that by attacking the science of it all and how it was handled he should be able to get some ground in that manner. I've seen countless reports which are damning to the NFL's conclusion that the Patriots cheated and I certainly hope that he's able to get some retribution out of all of this if he isn't responsible for it (which I believe but that doesn't make it true). Hopefully this will at least get all of it behind us and we can be back to the way things were and rub that victory in the Colt's face a little more.
